title: The Immaculate Heart of Mary
hook: the Saturday after the Sacred Heart, Mary's heart is honored
tomorrow: The first martyrs of Rome (30 June)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paulinus of Nola, the rich Roman who gave his wealth away and kept writing. Your line was the poet bishop. What gift did you give? Day one thousand three.

Shepherds crowd in around a manger at night, out of breath, talking over each other. Angels, they say. A sky full of them. Everyone who hears it is amazed. And in the middle of the noise, the young mother says nothing. Luke turns his camera to her face for one sentence and then moves on. On a Friday in the weeks after Pentecost, the Church honors the Sacred Heart of Jesus. On the next day, a Saturday, it turns to that quiet face, and the heart behind it. Today, the Immaculate Heart of Mary.
screen: `SHEPHERDS, OUT OF BREATH.` → `EVERYONE AMAZED.` → `THE MOTHER SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Kept, like something put away safely. Pondering, turning it over, the way you turn a stone in your hand. Luke says it again when Jesus is twelve, after he's found in the Temple: his mother kept all these words in her heart. Luke never gives us a speech from Mary at those moments. He gives us her heart, working. There's a third line, and it's harder. When the baby is presented in the Temple, an old man named Simeon blesses them and then says to Mary: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." That's why pictures of the Immaculate Heart often show a heart with a sword through it, or ringed with roses, or burning with flame. Love, and the cost of love, in one picture. A word about the name, because it trips people up. Immaculate here means without stain. Catholic teaching holds that Mary was kept free from sin from the first moment of her life; that's the Immaculate Conception, a separate feast in December. This day isn't about how she was conceived. It's about her heart: the inner life of a woman who said yes, kept watch, and stood at the cross. Over time the devotion grew, and some Catholics connect it with the reported apparitions of Mary at Fatima, in Portugal. Not every Christian keeps this devotion. Orthodox Christians honor Mary in their own ways, and some Protestants read these same verses as a picture of faith without a feast for her heart. For Catholics, putting the two hearts side by side, the Son's on Friday and the mother's on Saturday, says something plain: her heart was pointed toward his.
screen: `SHE KEPT THESE WORDS IN HER HEART.` · `A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.` · `IMMACULATE: WITHOUT STAIN.` · `TWO HEARTS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a mother's heart. Breathe out slowly. Bring to mind a mother you know: your own, or someone who mothered you, or a friend raising children right now. Think of what she might be carrying that she doesn't say out loud. A worry. A grief. A hope. Hold it with her, quietly. If you pray, you can entrust her to Mary, whose own heart held so much in silence. If you don't, simply wish her rest and company. The bell holds the time.
Immaculate Heart, the Catholic devotion to Mary's inner life, honored on the Saturday after the Sacred Heart.
Your line: her heart. Today, when you hear something big, don't answer straight away. Keep it, and turn it over before you speak. Day one thousand three.

howItsDone: The Church keeps the memorial of the Immaculate Heart of Mary on the Saturday after the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart; some Catholics pray the rosary on the day, and some keep a devotion of first Saturdays.

fork.setup: you're Mary. shepherds burst in with news of angels, and everyone is amazed. what does Luke say you do?
options: tell everyone what the angel told you.
keep these words and ponder them in your heart.
ask the shepherds to leave the baby to sleep.
fork.reveal: Luke gives no speech from Mary here: she keeps all these words, pondering them in her heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: a picture of a heart with flowers and a sword.
what it means: a feast for Mary's inner life, her keeping and pondering, and the cost of her love.
what a scholar hears: Luke 2:19 and 2:51 say she kept these words; Luke 2:35 is the sword; the memorial follows the Sacred Heart.

notes: Calendar: Sacred Heart on the Friday after the Second Sunday after Pentecost (index framing 'after Corpus Christi' simplified in the hook); confirm wording of 'the Friday after Corpus Christi', which holds where Corpus Christi is kept on Thursday.
'The devotion grew over centuries' and 'many Catholics connect it with ... Fatima': softened; confirm or cut 'many'.
Description of Orthodox and Protestant approaches ('many Protestants read these same verses...'): sweeping-claim risk under the claims rule; Keeper may prefer 'some Protestants'.
Immaculate Conception explanation: confirm wording ('kept free from sin from the first moment of her life').
'Jesus is twelve' is stated in Luke 2:42; kept.

Editor: 'the Friday after Corpus Christi' could be heard as the day after Corpus Christi (the Sacred Heart falls the following week), so the hook now says 'a Friday in the weeks after Pentecost'; Luke has a manger, not a stable; 'senator' in the review matched to day 1002's 'rich Roman'; doctrine framed as Catholic teaching.
